title: A live-imaging protocol to track cell movement in the Xenopus embryo
protocol: Inject adult female Xenopus laevis with Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (ChorulonR) subcutaneously into dorsal lymph sacs at 800 units per animal.
Collect eggs from females manually between 16 to 24 hours post-injection.
Euthanize adult male Xenopus laevis by immersing them in a benzocaine solution bath for 15 minutes.
Perform cervical section posterior to the skull after immersion in benzocaine solution to confirm euthanasia.
Collect sperm from euthanized males by explanting testes for in vitro fertilization.
Using dissection scissors, cut through the skin and abdominal muscles to open the lower abdominal cavity on the ventral side.
Locate the testes on the dorsal side of the cavity, on either side of the aorta, behind the fat bodies.
Cut out the testes and trim away any attached fat and viscera.
Transfer the testes at 4°C in 0.1× MBS for in vitro fertilization on the same day.
Note: Testes can be stored at 4°C in Leibovitz's L-15 Medium, GlutaMAX™ Supplement culture media for up to a week without significant loss of sperm viability.
Cut a quarter to a third of testis and crush it with a plastic microcentrifuge pestle in 0.5 mL of 0.1× MBS into a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube.
With a glass pipette, deposit the solution of crushed testis evenly on the eggs.
Use the plastic pestle to distribute the eggs into a monolayer on the Petri dish and wait for 5 minutes before covering them with 0.1× MBS for 1.5 hours.
De-jelly the fertilized eggs with gentle agitation for about 10 minutes in 2% cysteine in 0.1× MBS at pH 8.
Once the jelly-coat is dissolved and the eggs have started to pack, wash extensively in water to remove the cysteine.
Note: Prolonged exposure to cysteine will damage embryos.
Keep embryos in 0.1× MBS at 13°C, 18°C or 23°C until they reach the stage suitable for injection (8- or 16-cell).
Transfer embryos in Ficoll 4% in 1× MBS.
Prepare materials for microinjection using a Micro-manipulation and micro-injection device Nanoject II.
Pull glass needles from 1.14 mm (outer diameter) × 3.5" length × .53 mm (inner diameter) glass microcapillaries with a needle puller to achieve an inner tip diameter of 10–30 μm.
Back-fill the pulled glass needle with mineral oil using a Drummond syringe with a 30 gauge, 2" long blunt needle, avoiding air bubbles.
Mount the back-filled glass needle on a micro-manipulator.
Break the tip of the glass needle at an angle of 45° using surgical grade tweezers.
Prepare the injection mix short before injection with mRNA coding for mRFP (500 pg/blastomere) and pα-tub::GFP or pα-tub::LifeActGFP (50–60 pg/ blastomere).
Linearize both plasmids by NotI to increase the number of GFP-positive MCCs.
Optionally, co-inject constructs with morpholinos to deplete specific proteins for visualizing morphant cells with mRFP tracer or fluorescent morpholinos.
Adjust the concentration of each construct to the final volume to be injected in each blastomere.
Deposit a 1–3 μL drop of the injection mix on the bottom of a plastic Petri dish.
Load the injection mix into the glass needle by suction.
Inject the loaded construct mix under the apical surface of the ventral animal blastomeres (precursors of the non-neural ectoderm) of 8 cell- or 16 cell-stage embryos.
Transfer embryos in 2% Ficoll in 0.1× MBS and culture at 13°C.
Culture embryos in 0.1× MBS for 1–2 days at a preferred temperature (13°C–23°C).
Monitor the embryos until the first signs of stage 14 appear, when α-tub-driven expression of fluorescent proteins can be detected in the injected MCCs.
Incubate sibling injected embryos at different temperatures.
Note the developmental rates based on incubation temperature.
Prepare embryos cultured at 23°C for imaging 15 hours post-injection.
Prepare embryos cultured at 13°C for imaging 48 hours post-injection.
Inject at least 10–15 embryos per condition to account for potential sample loss.
(Optional) Add pharmacological inhibitors to the culture medium from stage 12 onwards.
Sort fluorescently labeled embryos under a stereomicroscope when they reach stage 14.
Prepare the embedding medium for live imaging.
Melt 0.8% low melting point agar in 0.1× MBS using microwave or 37°C water bath.
Wait until the solution cools below 40°C before use.
Delimit a roughly 2 cm² area chamber onto a 24*40 mm coverslip with silicon grease, without completely closing it.
Add 3-4 drops of molten agar to the chamber containing the embryos.
Embed the embryos between two coverslips for live imaging.
Melt agar with a 37°C water bath.
Delineate a chamber of roughly 2cm² area onto a 24×40 mm coverslip using a 10 mL needle-less syringe filled with silicon grease.
Fill the chamber with 3–4 drops of molten agar using a flame-polished glass Pasteur pipette or plastic pipette.
Drop 4–5 selected embryos in molten agar using a flame-polished glass Pasteur pipette or plastic pipette.
Position embryos under a fluorescent dissecting microscope such that regions richest in GFP-positive MCCs face upwards.
Quickly seal the silicon grease chamber with a second coverslip before the agar sets.
Rotate embryos back into a favorable position by gently sliding the two coverslips against each other if they roll during sealing.
Press gently the two coverslips to slightly flatten the embryos without crushing them for optimal imaging.
Start live imaging experiment immediately after embedding the embryos.
Position the coverslip ‘sandwich’ in the imaging chamber of the Nikon Roper spinning-disk Eclipse Ti inverted confocal microscope.
Stabilize the chamber at 23°C to reduce developmental variability between experiments.
Choose the objective.
Select the optimal field with mercury lamp HBO 50 W fluorescent illumination.
Set up microscope for z-stack time-lapse acquisition: 20 μm-deep Z sections; z-step = 0.5–0.7 μm; 2 frames averaging; time interval 30 s–2 min (depending on the number of channels used).
Adjust exposure time and laser power to the fluorescence intensity of the different channels.
Select a field of interest.
Set your stacks range taking as reference the 561 nm channel and the surface of the outer layer cells for the most apical z.
Use the 491 nm channel, which labels the MCCs within the inner layer for the most basal z.
Launch time-lapse acquisition for 2–10 h.
Adjust manually the X, Y and Z axes whenever necessary using the joystick Nikon TI-S-EJOY system.
Process raw data obtained with spinning-disk confocal time-lapse imaging.
Use imageJ/Fiji free software for image and movie visualization.
Convert z-stacks from confocal video microscopy into single plane projection by maximum intensity or sum intensity projection.
Process each channel separately with the optimized z-section corresponding to the outer/inner layer cell staining.
Track a single vertex frame by frame using the “manual tracking” Fiji plugin to extract its coordinates as reference for movie stabilization.
Quantify tracked vertex drift at frame level and correct it using a Python 3 script.
Use the “Image Stabilizer” Fiji plugin, which implements the Lucas-Kanade algorithm, to further stabilize the movie.
Open the stabilized movie for analysis.
Create one track per MCC in the movie using the "manual tracking" Fiji plugin.
Manually click on the centroid of each MCC from the beginning to the end to track its migratory behavior throughout the movie.
